title: Garment, toy companies go full throttle as US buyers look beyond China
summary: Garment and toy makers are accelerating production and shifting sourcing away from China as US buyers diversify their supply chains amid tariffs, forced labour probes and changing trade policies, boosting opportunities in countries like India.
content:
Garment and toy companies are ramping up production and expanding sourcing outside China as US buyers increasingly seek to diversify supply chains and reduce concentration risk.

A mix of commercial and policy factors is driving the trend. Rising costs in China, heightened scrutiny over forced labour, proposed additional US tariffs and broader geopolitical tensions have prompted major buyers to look for alternative suppliers. The result is faster capacity buildout, retooling of factories and more aggressive procurement strategies across South and Southeast Asia, Latin America and parts of Eastern Europe.

India has emerged as a prominent beneficiary of this shift. Recent policy moves and trade discussions underscore how New Delhi is positioning itself to capture more manufacturing investment. The government has been active on multiple trade fronts, from pressing the US to reconsider proposed additional tariffs to working with the EU on finalising FTA legal scrubbing, while also adjusting customs and import rules under new trade pacts. At the same time, authorities are tightening scrutiny of certain imports and emphasising compliance to address buyers' concerns about inputs and supply chain transparency.

Other reports show that despite tariff tensions, some Indian sectors such as auto parts continue to hold strong export ties with the US, reflecting an ability to adapt to shifting trade dynamics. Bilateral and multilateral negotiations, investment pledges and new pacts with partners including Russia, Israel and European nations are contributing to a more favourable backdrop for manufacturers looking to scale up.

For garment and toy suppliers, the practical response has been clear: expand capacity, invest in compliance and traceability, and shorten lead times. Countries such as Vietnam, Bangladesh, Mexico and India are seeing increased orders and investment inquiries, prompting faster hiring, factory upgrades and logistics improvements.

The near term could remain disruptive as buyers rebalance supplier networks, but the longer-term picture points to a more diversified global manufacturing landscape. Companies and countries that can deliver reliable capacity, transparent compliance and competitive costs are likely to capture the bulk of the new business as US buyers look beyond China.
